title: Uber Moves Beyond CPU Cores with Performance-Aware Scheduling for Stateful Workloads
gist: Uber's Odin platform, which manages about 5M CPU cores, now allocates CPU in Normalized Compute Units weighted by each server type's measured performance (baseline 100, up to about 190), instead of treating all cores as equal. On about 1.4M auto-scaled cores this narrowed Kafka utilisation spread from about 8 to about 3 percentage points and cut Kafka CPU allocation by about 8%.

insights.claim: Uber's Odin stateful orchestration platform manages about 5 million CPU cores across on-premises data centres and public clouds, spanning multiple x86 generations and ARM processors.
insights.so_what: Shows the scale and hardware mix behind Uber's hybrid on-prem and cloud infrastructure strategy.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi

insights.claim: At Uber, single-threaded performance differs by almost a factor of two between the fastest and slowest cores, so the same workload needs very different numbers of physical cores depending on where it runs.
insights.so_what: Treating a core as a fixed unit is a poor measure of compute in mixed fleets, which complicates cloud pricing and capacity planning.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi

insights.claim: Load balancing can absorb hardware differences for stateless services, but not for stateful systems, where requests must reach the server holding a given shard. A leader using more than ten times its followers' CPU can hit resource pressure simply by moving to slower hardware.
insights.so_what: Databases and streaming systems carry hidden reliability risk in mixed hardware fleets.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi

insights.claim: Uber's Normalized Compute Units give each server type a performance factor against an older-generation baseline of 100, with some newer servers approaching 190. Factors are set during hardware qualification and refined with production data.
insights.so_what: A per-generation performance multiplier indicates how much more compute newer hardware delivers per core.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi

insights.claim: Performance factors differ by technology: Uber's Kafka measurements showed substantially different results across ARM, older on-prem and newer x86 hardware, so Uber relies on production measurements over synthetic benchmarks.
insights.so_what: How ARM compares to x86 depends on the workload, so headline benchmarks can mislead hardware purchasing.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi

insights.claim: Kubernetes treats a CPU unit as an absolute quantity of CPU time regardless of hardware. That keeps workload definitions portable but cannot express the relative performance of processor generations, which Uber's NCU model adds.
insights.so_what: A gap in mainstream orchestration that vendors or cloud providers could fill with performance-aware resource units.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi

insights.claim: Across about 1.4 million auto-scaled Odin cores, Kafka's CPU utilisation spread between server types fell from about 8 to about 3 percentage points; the hottest hardware went from about 50% to about 10% above the coldest.
insights.so_what: More even utilisation lets operators run higher average load safely and buy less hardware.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi

insights.claim: Performance-aware allocation cut Uber's total Kafka CPU allocation by about 8%, with most of the savings on faster hardware, where capacity is more valuable.
insights.so_what: Shows that software-level efficiency can defer capex at hyperscale.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
